slides.title: Why stool is examined
bullets: Stool is the end product of life processes formed in the gastrointestinal tract: water, food remains, intestinal secretions, bile-pigment products and bacteria.
The test helps to assess the enzymatic activity of the stomach and bowel through how well food is digested, and the evacuation function of the bowel.
It gives information about inflammation, the intestinal microbiota and pathogenic micro-organisms, and about protozoa and helminth eggs.
The general analysis has three parts: macroscopic, chemical and microscopic examination.

slides.title: Collecting and delivering the specimen
bullets: Stool is collected into a special container after spontaneous defaecation; it must not be mixed with urine.
Before a general analysis the patient eats food with a set content of protein, fat and carbohydrate for 3–4 bowel movements.
Stool obtained after an enema, laxatives, suppositories, castor or paraffin oil, or drugs that change its colour (iron, bismuth, barium) is unsuitable.

slides.title: Collecting and delivering the specimen
bullets: Kurbonova says to examine stool within 8–12 hours of defaecation in a clean dry container; Aripov et al. say to deliver it at once or within 10–12 hours, kept in a refrigerator; for the exact time follow the laboratory’s instructions.

slides.title: Equipment and reagents
bullets: Porcelain dishes, glass rods, Petri dishes, slides and cover glasses, test tubes, rack, microscope.
Lugol’s solution (in the manual: 1 g iodine, 2 g potassium iodide, 50 mL distilled water) — to detect starch.
0.5% methylene blue solution — to tell neutral fat from fatty acids.

slides.title: Equipment and reagents
bullets: 30% acetic acid solution — for the preparation that detects salts of fatty acids (soaps).
Lugol’s solution is made fresh every month because iodine breaks down on long storage.

slides.title: Macroscopic assessment and reaction
bullets: 1. Check that the details on the container label match the request form; examine specimens one at a time.
2. Assess amount, consistency, shape, colour and smell.
3. Note admixtures visible to the naked eye: mucus, blood, pus, undigested food remains, worms or their fragments.
4. To measure the reaction, wet universal indicator paper with distilled water and touch it to several places in the stool.

slides.title: Macroscopic assessment and reaction
bullets: 5. After 2–3 minutes compare the colour of the paper with the scale (Kurbonova also mentions diagnostic test strips).
6. Record the results accurately and completely.

slides.title: Macroscopic findings
rows: About 150–200 g a day (Kurbonova); 120–200 g (Aripov et al.)
More — impaired digestion, diarrhoea; less — constipation, poor intake
Mushy or liquid — faster peristalsis, inflammation; “sheep” stool — constipation; ribbon-like — rectal spasm or obstruction

slides.title: Macroscopic findings
rows: White — bile-duct obstruction; black — bleeding from the upper tract; red — from the lower tract. Food and drugs also change the colour
Acid — much carbohydrate, fermentation; alkaline — much protein or putrefaction

slides.title: Macroscopic findings
rows: No mucus, blood, pus or undigested food remains
Mucus — bowel inflammation; pus — severe bowel inflammation; fat — pancreatic insufficiency

slides.title: Slides for microscopy
rows: A drop of stool emulsion on a slide, covered with a cover glass
Food remains (muscle fibres, connective tissue, fibre, fat), mucus, cells, eggs and cysts
An equal drop of Lugol’s solution is mixed into a drop of emulsion
A drop of emulsion is mixed with a drop of 30% acetic acid; heated to boiling if needed
Salts of fatty acids (soaps); drops forming on heating mean soaps

slides.title: Slides for microscopy
rows: A drop of emulsion is mixed with a drop of 0.5% methylene blue
Fatty-acid drops turn blue; neutral fat stays colourless
Separated mucus, pus or a tissue fragment is placed on the slide and covered
White cells, red cells, epithelium, tumour elements, protozoa

slides.title: Microscopy
bullets: 1. The slides are examined with the 10× and 40× objectives.
2. In the native slide look first, against the detritus background, for undigested protein and carbohydrate remains, fat drops, crystals, mucus and cells.
3. In the Lugol slide assess starch and iodophilic flora; in the methylene blue slide, fatty-acid drops.

slides.title: Microscopy
bullets: 4. White and red cells are counted per field; everything found (including eggs and cysts) is recorded.
5. Slides III–V (acetic acid, methylene blue, mucus-pus) are prepared in large laboratories under the supervision of the doctor-technologist.

slides.title: Food remains
rows: Meat is poorly digested: deficiency of gastric juice or pancreatic function, faster peristalsis, fermentation and putrefaction
Food evacuated too early; deficiency of gastric juice or pancreatic function; poor chewing. Bits of cartilage and bone are not pathology

slides.title: Food remains
rows: None (fatty acids may occur in infants); soaps in very small amounts
Too little bile, pancreatic insufficiency, putrefactive and fermentative dyspepsia, faster peristalsis
A little digested; undigested in varying amounts
Much digested fibre: no gastric acid, fast evacuation, disturbed bowel flora

slides.title: Cells, mucus and crystals
rows: Putrefactive and fermentative dyspepsia, colitis with constipation; bowel epithelium — inflammation of the colon; many neutrophils — bacterial dysentery, eosinophils — amoebic dysentery
Bowel inflammation (dysentery, ulcerative colitis, intestinal tuberculosis), rupture of a perianal abscess, breakdown of a tumour

slides.title: Cells, mucus and crystals
rows: Unchanged — haemorrhoids, ulcerative colitis, colon tumour, anal fissures; broken-down or “ghosts” — bleeding from the upper tract

slides.title: Cells, mucus and crystals
rows: Calcium oxalate — much vegetable food, low gastric acidity; triple phosphate — putrefactive dyspepsia; Charcot–Leyden — allergic inflammation, helminthiasis; cholesterol — no diagnostic value; haematoidin — after bowel bleeding
Plenty of saprophytic flora (E. coli, bifidobacteria)
A shift in flora and growth of pathogenic flora — dysbacteriosis (often after antibiotics)

slides.title: Coprological picture: a comparison
rows: Muscle fibres few, with or without striation; moderate digested fibre; single calcium oxalate crystals
Many muscle fibres with ragged edges (creatorrhoea), connective tissue, digested fibre, oxalate crystals
Stool with a shiny greasy coat; with methylene blue the neutral-fat drops stay colourless

slides.title: Coprological picture: a comparison
rows: Colourless stool; many fatty-acid drops or needles; on heating the needles turn into drops
Much digested fibre and starch; reaction shifted to acid; stool mushy and foamy
Strongly alkaline reaction; triple phosphate crystals, undigested muscle fibres, exudate and mucus

slides.title: Sources of error
bullets: An unsuitable specimen (after an enema, laxative or oil, colouring drugs, mixed with urine) spoils the result.
If the preparation regimen (food of a set composition) was not followed, linking the food remains found to a digestive disorder is unreliable.
Neutral fat and fatty acids cannot be told apart by appearance alone: methylene blue stains only fatty-acid drops.
Iodine breaks down when Lugol’s solution is stored for long — make it fresh every month.
Some findings have no diagnostic value (for example cholesterol crystals, bits of cartilage and bone) — do not read them as a sign of disease.

slides.title: Occult blood: preparation and tests not covered
bullets: Before a test for occult blood, meat, fish and sausage and iron-containing drugs are excluded (Kurbonova: meat, fish, sausage for 3 days, iron for 4–5 days; no tooth-brushing for 3 days). The manual also excludes green vegetables, tomatoes and eggs.
In the Aripova book meat, fish and drugs containing iodine, bromine or iron are excluded for 3 days, and the sample is taken on the fourth day.

slides.title: Occult blood: preparation and tests not covered
bullets: The guaiac (with ether), benzidine and Gregersen tests from the Kurbonova textbook, and the Schmidt reaction for stercobilin with mercuric chloride, are not included in this protocol: they rely on flammable ether, a poisonous mercury salt or outdated reagents.
Occult blood and stercobilin are measured by the laboratory’s approved method or by the instructions of a ready-made test.

slides.title: Safety
bullets: Stool specimens may contain pathogenic micro-organisms — parasites, bacteria and viruses; handle them with the usual precautions.
Wear single-use gloves; wash the hands after work.
Use containers with a tightly fitting lid; paper, cardboard and matchboxes are not suitable.
Disinfect used containers, slides and instruments according to the regulation in force.
Take care with the open flame when heating over a spirit lamp.

slides.title: Stool examination (coprology)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Stool (clean, dry container; no urine, water or toilet paper)  ·  Units: g/24 h

What it is used for: Stool tests look for blood, bacteria, parasites or signs of disease — for example, when looking for the cause of diarrhea. Finding white blood cells on microscopy helps tell whether diarrhea is due to inflammation in the gut.

Physiology: The normal brown colour of stool comes from bile salts released by the liver. Absorbing fat needs bile, pancreatic enzymes and a normal small intestine; when absorption fails, stool fat rises (steatorrhea).

slides.title: Stool examination (coprology)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Interpreting the result · 1/5
bullets: Pale or clay-coloured stool may point to a problem in the biliary system: a liver infection that reduces bile production, or blocked bile flow out of the liver. Jaundice and dark urine often occur with it.

slides.title: Stool examination (coprology)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Interpreting the result · 2/5
bullets: Black, tarry stool (melena) most often means bleeding in the upper GI tract — oesophagus, stomach or first part of the small intestine; the blood darkens as it is digested. Red, fresh blood in stool most often comes from the lower GI tract (colon, rectum or anus).

slides.title: Stool examination (coprology)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Interpreting the result · 3/5
bullets: White blood cells in stool mean there is inflammation in the digestive tract. This helps rule out viral infections, certain bacteria and most parasites. Causes of inflammatory diarrhea include some bacterial infections (C. difficile, Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter), inflammatory bowel disease and Entamoeba histolytica; further tests show the exact cause.

slides.title: Stool examination (coprology)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Interpreting the result · 4/5
bullets: Stool fat is checked under a microscope on a single sample, or measured in all stool collected over 24 hours (sometimes 3 days). MedlinePlus gives less than 7 g of fat per 24 hours as normal for the quantitative test. Reduced fat absorption occurs with celiac disease, chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, Crohn disease, biliary strictures or gallstones, and other conditions.

slides.title: Stool examination (coprology)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Interpreting the result · 5/5
bullets: A Gram-stained stool smear is read for the colour, size and shape of bacteria. A normal result shows only the usual ("friendly") gut bacteria. An abnormal result means an intestinal infection may be present; stool culture and other tests help find the cause.

slides.title: Stool examination (coprology)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/4
bullets: Pre-analytics: Stool is caught in a clean, dry container or on special paper or plastic wrap over the toilet; never take the sample from toilet water, and keep urine, water and toilet paper out. Label the container with name, date and time, close it tightly and wash hands with soap. If it cannot be returned right away, refrigerate it. For children in diapers, plastic wrap is placed inside the diaper.

slides.title: Stool examination (coprology)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/4
bullets: Before a quantitative fat test, eat a normal diet with about 100 g of fat a day for 3 days, then collect all stool over 24 hours (sometimes 3 days) in the containers provided.

slides.title: Stool examination (coprology)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/4
bullets: Interferences: Black stool can also come from black licorice, blueberries, blood sausage, iron pills, activated charcoal or bismuth medicines rather than blood; beets and red-coloured foods can make stool look reddish. In these cases the stool is tested chemically for blood.
Enemas, laxatives, mineral oil and too little dietary fat before and during collection interfere with the fat test.

slides.title: Stool examination (coprology)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 4/4
bullets: Limitations: A negative result cannot rule out inflammation: white cells do not last long in stool and may break apart before testing. The test cannot name the exact cause of diarrhea; when the picture is unclear, a stool calprotectin test may be ordered.
